title: Virtual Private Clouds (VPC), Subnets & Routing
summary: Design multi-tier public and private VPC topologies using CIDR math, Internet Gateways, NAT Gateways, and stateful Security Groups.
learningObjectives: Partition a VPC CIDR block into isolated public and private Availability Zone subnets
Trace packet flow cleanly through Internet Gateways, NAT Gateways, Security Groups, and Route Tables

sections.heading: 1. Multi-Tier VPC Isolation & Packet Flow
sections.content:
A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) gives you a logically isolated virtual network (e.g., `10.0.0.0/16`). Security best practice isolates infrastructure tiers across Public Subnets (holding strictly Load Balancers and NAT Gateways routed to an Internet Gateway `0.0.0.0/0 -> igw-...`) and Private Subnets (holding Application nodes and Databases with NO direct public IP or route from the open internet).

If an application instance inside a private subnet needs to call external vendor APIs or download OS patches, its route table points `0.0.0.0/0` to a NAT Gateway residing in a public subnet—enabling outbound egress while blocking unsolicited inbound internet scans completely.

codeExamples.code:
Internet <--> [Internet Gateway] <--> Public Subnet (ALB + NAT Gateway)
                                           | (Security Group: 443 allowed from ALB only)
                                           v
                                     Private App Subnet (ECS / EC2 App)
                                           | (Security Group: 5432 allowed from App SG only)
                                           v
                                     Private DB Subnet (Managed PostgreSQL)
codeExamples.explanation: Defense-in-depth subnet tiering keeps databases completely unreachable from public IP space.

keyPoints: Security Groups are stateful firewalls bound to instances/ENIs (allowing return packets automatically).
Network ACLs (NACLs) are stateless subnet boundaries filtering explicit inbound and outbound rules.
Never open database ports (`5432`, `3306`, `27017`) or SSH (`22`) to `0.0.0.0/0`.
commonMistakes: Launching PostgreSQL inside a public subnet with `0.0.0.0/0` access during initial setup and forgetting to close it.

sections.heading: 2. CIDR Capacity Math & Route Table Verification
sections.content: Before creating subnets, engineers validate host capacity using CIDR prefix length (`2^(32 - prefix)`). Always leave comfortable IP headroom in Kubernetes/container subnets so rolling upgrades can spawn surge pods before draining old ones.

codeExamples.code:
# Example VPC Allocation Plan (10.0.0.0/16 -> 65,536 IPs)
# Public Subnet AZ-A:  10.0.1.0/24   (256 IPs -> route 0.0.0.0/0 to igw-main)
# Public Subnet AZ-B:  10.0.2.0/24   (256 IPs -> route 0.0.0.0/0 to igw-main)
# Private App AZ-A:    10.0.16.0/22  (1,024 IPs -> route 0.0.0.0/0 to nat-az-a)
# Private DB AZ-A:     10.0.32.0/24  (256 IPs -> route strictly local VPC only)

# Calculate usable hosts cleanly with Python ipaddress:
python3 -c "import ipaddress; n=ipaddress.ip_network('10.0.16.0/22'); print('Total:', n.num_addresses, 'Range:', n.network_address, '-', n.broadcast_address)"
codeExamples.explanation: Using non-overlapping `/22` app subnets ensures rolling container deployments never run out of ENI private IP addresses.

keyPoints: Reference source Security Group IDs (e.g., `sg-app-tier`) rather than static IP addresses inside database firewall rules.
commonMistakes: Sizing Kubernetes worker subnets as tiny `/28` ranges (only 16 total IPs -> 11 usable in cloud), stalling auto-scaling immediately.

exercises.title: Design a Zero-Exposure 3-Tier VPC Subnet Plan
exercises.objective: Architect non-overlapping VPC CIDR blocks and pinpoint Security Group rules isolating backend databases.
exercises.description: Given VPC `172.16.0.0/16`, allocate 2 public subnets, 2 private application subnets supporting 400 hosts each, and 2 private DB subnets across AZ-a and AZ-b.
instructions: Select appropriate CIDR blocks (`/24` vs `/23` vs `/22`) avoiding overlap.
Define routes for public subnets vs private subnets.
Specify the exact Security Group rule allowing app servers to query PostgreSQL port 5432.
exercises.starterCode:
# VPC 172.16.0.0/16 Plan
Public AZ-A: 172.16.1.0/24 -> Route 0.0.0.0/0 -> ...
Private App AZ-A (needs 400+ hosts): ...
DB Security Group Rule: Source = ... Port = ...
hints: A `/24` has only 256 IPs (insufficient for 400+ hosts); `/23` provides 512 IPs.
Databases should only accept TCP 5432 from the App Security Group ID.
exercises.submissionRequirements: Complete all checklist items, test assumptions, and document verification rationale.
evaluationCriteria: Addresses the root architectural/technical challenge accurately
Follows defensive industry standards and edge-case validation
exercises.solutionExplanation: `/23` yields 512 IPs fitting 400+ pods cleanly, while referencing the App Security Group restricts database traffic purely to verified app nodes.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Why does placing application containers inside a Private Subnet with a NAT Gateway enhance security over Public Subnets?

options.text: Instances have no public IPv4 address reachable for unsolicited inbound scans while still able to initiate outbound API/package calls cleanly
NAT Gateways automatically encrypt SQL queries inside JSON
Private subnets turn off CPU hyperthreading

knowledgeChecks.explanation: NAT Gateways allow initiated outbound sessions while blocking unsolicited inbound internet connections.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: How many total IPv4 addresses exist inside a `/26` CIDR subnet block?
Which firewall construct operates statelessly at the subnet boundary evaluating inbound and outbound ACL numbers separately?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: NACLs are stateless packet filters evaluated at subnet edges; Security Groups are stateful.

recap: You built secure multi-tier VPC topologies, calculated CIDR ranges reliably, and separated stateful vs stateless cloud firewalls.
